encounters.cc: Two-week history of worsening blurry vision, floaters, and flashes in the left eye

lines: Two-week history of worsening blurry vision, floaters, and flashes in the left eye
He says the problem began as “little specks floating around” that have gradually grown into large dark patches obscuring his sight.
He also reports occasional flashes of light and describes his vision as “looking through a fogged-up window.” He has mild discomfort but no severe eye pain.
Today, he says his main concern is that he is afraid of going completely blind.
He explains that his vision problems are much worse in his left eye but are beginning to affect the right eye as well.

The patient has a long history of HIV infection diagnosed 12 years ago.
He was initially prescribed antiretroviral therapy but has been inconsistently adherent, often stopping his medications during times of instability.
He admits that he has not taken his HIV medicines in over a year.
His last clinic visit was more than 18 months ago.
- Incision and drainage of left arm abscess, 2019
- No other known surgeries

NKDA
He was once married, but his wife passed away 10 years ago from complications of breast cancer.
He became estranged from his only brother after a series of family disputes, and both of his parents died in his twenties.
He has struggled with depression since these losses.
He began using intravenous heroin in his thirties, which worsened his social isolation.
Over the past decade, he has been intermittently homeless, often sleeping in shelters or outdoors.
For the past several winters, he has been staying under a bridge near Harvard Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he would light small fires at night to stay warm.
He sometimes traded belongings for food and occasionally worked day labor jobs.
Despite these hardships, he has had a few passions in life.
He enjoys writing short stories, especially about his experiences traveling across New England.
He once told a physician that he loved the sense of freedom he felt when hitchhiking between small towns.
He also has a deep interest in jazz and would occasionally busk with a harmonica outside small cafes in Boston.
The patient admits to past alcohol and cocaine use but says that heroin was his main struggle.
He has been on and off methadone treatment but relapsed frequently.
He has not used intravenous drugs in the last year, though he continues to smoke cigarettes daily.
He denies recent headaches, focal weakness, or seizures.
He has had no recent fevers, chills, or weight gain but admits to losing 15 pounds over the past 6 months.
His vital signs are stable.
On examination, he is thin, with temporal wasting.
He appears disheveled but cooperative.
Ocular exam reveals cotton-wool exudates and hemorrhagic lesions along the retinal periphery, resembling a “pizza pie” or “flame-shaped” pattern.
Pupillary light reflexes are intact.
The remainder of the neurological exam is nonfocal.
Laboratory studies from today show a CD4 count of 35/mm³.

encounters.cc: Fever, chills, and severe sore throat preventing oral intake

lines: Fever, chills, and severe sore throat preventing oral intake

The patient is a 41-year-old male with HIV infection with AIDS (CD4 count <50 cells/mm³), treatment-refractory schizophrenia, and a history of CMV esophagitis diagnosed in January 2020, who is poorly adherent to antiretroviral therapy and MAC prophylaxis.
He is brought to the emergency department by a community outreach volunteer because of fever, chills, and sore throat.
He says that the throat pain started 3 days ago and has been getting progressively worse.
He also reports fatigue, malaise, and painful swallowing that prevents him from eating much solid food.
He denies cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath.
Over the past week, however, he has felt progressively more fatigued.
He developed subjective fevers, chills, and oral discomfort.
Two days ago he noticed painful ulcerations on his gums and tongue.
Today, he feels too weak to walk long distances and accepted the help of a volunteer who insisted he be brought to the hospital.

His past psychiatric history is extensive, including diagnoses of schizophrenia, depression, and generalized anxiety disorder.
He has been hospitalized multiple times in psychiatric wards since his late teens, often due to auditory hallucinations and disorganized behavior.
- Incision and drainage of left arm abscess, 2019
- No other known surgeries
Over the years, he has been tried on multiple medications including haloperidol, risperidone, quetiapine, fluoxetine, and lithium.
Due to persistent refractory psychosis, his care team eventually initiated clozapine therapy, which he has been taking for the past year.
He is also prescribed valproic acid as a mood stabilizer, lorazepam as needed for agitation, and sertraline for comorbid depressive symptoms.
He admits that his lifestyle makes it difficult to keep up with medical appointments, and he often skips his medications depending on availability.
Despite these challenges, he has continued clozapine almost daily because, in his words, "it's the only one that really makes the voices quiet."
Home Medications:
- Bictegravir/Tenofovir alafenamide/Emtricitabine (Biktarvy) 50/25/200 mg orally daily, poorly adherent
- Azithromycin 1200 mg orally weekly for MAC prophylaxis, poorly adherent

He lost touch with his family years ago after repeated conflicts and strained relationships, and he currently has no fixed residence.
He usually sleeps outside near a convenience store in Brickell, Miami.
He describes this as "the safest spot I could find" and says that store clerks occasionally give him food.
On days when he does not stay in Brickell, he sometimes travels to Wynwood and sleeps near an abandoned building, where he feels somewhat shielded from the rain.
He frequently wanders shopping streets in both neighborhoods, asking strangers for spare change.
He does not smoke cigarettes but occasionally drinks alcohol when he has access to it.
He does not use illicit drugs currently but has a remote history of marijuana and cocaine use.
On review of systems, he denies chest pain, hemoptysis, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or skin rashes.
His temperature is 38.9 °C (102 °F), blood pressure 108/65 mm Hg, pulse 110/min, and respiratory rate 18/min.
Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air.
On physical examination, he appears tired and somewhat disheveled.
He has multiple tender oral ulcers and pharyngeal erythema.
No cervical lymphadenopathy is appreciated.
Cardiovascular and pulmonary exams are unremarkable.
Abdominal exam reveals no hepatosplenomegaly.
There are no skin rashes or petechiae.
Further questioning reveals that he has not had a complete blood count performed in several months.
His care team is concerned about a medication-induced complication.
